comment.body:
Now for the unexpected and out of the box proposal that sidesteps the problem entirely. Have you heard the good word about [MetaLink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalink)?

This is a bit like torrents, but designed as a download accelerator mechanism. You get rather high reliability of your download, since it includes chunkwise hashing. You can download individual chunks in parallel from various geodistributed CDNs (forgejo probably does not need this). You can detect corruption and partial downloads and resume arbitrarily anywhere since most of the content you already downloaded fits into a chunk that can be verified to be intact.

You could serve MetaLink to supporting clients -- mirrorbrain / mirrorcache do this -- and I suppose you could store them directly rather than serving via a CDN. This provides dubious security benefits as a free side effect of excellent corruption detection and resume support that the user doing the download doesn't have to think about.

comment.body:
@crueter wrote in https://codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo/issues/14178#issuecomment-28371422:

> The fundamental tenet of security is to trust nobody. ;)

This is a suitably vague statement that elides a definition of trust and also one of security. One cannot solve the fundamental tenets of security through the mechanism of picking arbitrary technological algorithms out of a lottery, then finding a way to build a feature that "uses that algorithm" (in this case the winning lottery entry was "sha256").

So we're back to the original question, what is the *goal* of installing a digest functionality into the downloads page? Without a goal we don't know what direction we're heading and certainly cannot make any progress.

The original proposal basically suggested the goal is to detect when, due to a network interruption, the file was truncated / download aborted / some other form of accidental corruption. But download clients tend to be pretty good at catching that already. Would it suffice if forgejo explicitly provided digests that disavow all uses other than corruption detection? Let us say:

> THE CRC32 DIGEST IS PROVIDED “AS IS”, WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND, EXPRESS OR IMPLIED, INCLUDING BUT NOT LIMITED TO THE WARRANTIES OF MERCHANTABILITY, FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR OR INDEED ANY PURPOSE, AND SECURITY. IN NO EVENT SHALL THE UPLOADERS OR SUPPLIERS BE LIABLE FOR ANY CLAIM, DAMAGES OR OTHER LIABILITY, WHETHER IN AN ACTION OF CONTRACT, TORT OR OTHERWISE, ARISING FROM, OUT OF OR IN CONNECTION WITH THE DIGEST OR TRUST THAT THE DIGEST MEANS ANYTHING OR THE USE OR OTHER DEALINGS IN THE DIGEST.

And anyone who assumes that a crc32 digest is intended to be a security mechanism will have had numerous warnings signs before they got that far.

This is "good enough" for corruption detection.

...

If the intent of the digest is for security, then we return to the wisdom of "trust nobody" and especially do not trust the forge itself. This is the reason why, for security reasons, I refuse to trust digests on GitHub and would likewise refuse to trust them on forgejo.

If we disregard "trust nobody" and decide to trust somebody, namely, the forge, but we are worried about the forge using a non-trustworthy CDN, then I would worry the html page and/or the JavaScript may be manipulated by the CDN to return a variety of suspicious things including a malicious checksum too. If that CDN is cloudflare I'm *extra* worried.

So...

@eschwartz wrote in https://codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo/issues/14178#issuecomment-22908721:

> It sounds like the major reason to add it is "for feature parity with github since github offers them" (and "adding it causes no harm"), but... is that really a reason?

> also has to be applied to other features in Forgejo to no longer make the assumption it can trust the filesystem, external services etc.

The fundamental tenet of security is to trust nobody. ;)
